column4: God makes iron pliable for David; the next ayah directs him to make armor. This gives the section's spear-and-arrow craft a concrete Qur'anic scene of material shaped for use.
David is told to make linked armor, measure its links (“وَقَدِّرْ فِي السَّرْدِ”), and do righteous work; this directly joins measured craftsmanship to صَالِحًا, the section's sound-work theme.
David is taught to make armor that protects people in battle; it is a specific parallel to the section's well-fashioned spear and arrow as useful crafted objects.
Noah is commanded to build the ship under God's watch and revelation; this stages the section's human craftsman at work under divine direction.
Noah is told to construct the ship under God's eyes and inspiration; the ayah supplies another specific act of making, akin to the section's measured craft.
Noah builds the ship while his people mock him; this neighbor adds the response of denial to the craft scene, like the section's human forgetting the maker despite being carefully made.

When the wall is about to fall, the traveler “فَأَقَامَهُ” (sets it upright); the section's root ق و م is glossed through straightening, and this is a specific act of repair that restores a structure.
The wall protected treasure for two orphans until they matured, because their father was righteous; this later explanation completes 18:77's repair and links sound work to care and eventual benefit.
The mountains are described as a work of God who “أَتْقَنَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ”; this is a direct formulation of the masterful finishing that the section draws from أَحْسَنَ.
Abraham asks whether his people worship what they carve; the section's human craftsman and crafted arrow meet here in a reversal where made objects are wrongly worshipped.
The ayah says God created the makers and what they make; it sharpens the section's boundary between human workmanship and the divine making of the human.

The command “أَحْسِن كَمَا أَحْسَنَ اللَّهُ إِلَيْكَ” joins God's good work toward a person to that person's good work, then forbids فساد; it closely matches the section's crafted human, صالحات, and soundness against corruption.
The passage condemns those who cheat in measure; this is the defective opposite of the section's measured hide and straightened tools.
The defrauders take full measure for themselves; the ayah specifies the self-serving half of the corrupt measuring scene.
They short people when measuring or weighing for them; this completes the concrete measure-and-defect contrast developed from the section's craft lexicon.
The passage asks whether the defrauders expect to be raised for a great day; this neighbor connects corrupt measure to the judgment question that follows the section's making and work.
The passage asks whether God created people from lowly fluid; this begins a direct account of material becoming human, alongside the section's خ ل ق gloss of measuring before cutting.
The fluid is placed in a secure resting place; this is a specific intermediate stage in the making process.
The placement lasts to a known measure (“إِلَىٰ قَدَرٍ مَّعْلُومٍ”); it directly connects human formation to the section's measured making.
The passage says God measured the process and calls Him the best measurer; this is a compact direct parallel to the section's reading of خ ل ق as straight measure.
The human is made from a mixed drop and furnished with hearing and sight for a test; the ayah connects careful formation to the capacities by which the work is judged.
God shows the way, leaving the human grateful or ungrateful; this makes the moral outcome of a well-made human explicit.
The human is given two eyes; this begins a list of fitted bodily faculties that makes the section's workmanship image concrete.
The tongue and lips continue that list of formed faculties, each suited to the human's use.
After naming these faculties, the ayah says God guided the human to two paths; it connects the fitted form to a choice between outcomes.
People emerge from their mothers knowing nothing and are given hearing, sight and hearts so that they may be grateful; this shows the maker furnishing the human with capacities and a purpose.
Noah says God created people “أَطْوَارًا,” in stages; this is a direct repeated formulation of the section's staged craftsmanship.
Heavens and earth are created, then human life is made a test of who is best in deeds; this joins divine making to the section's concern for the quality of human work.
Earth's adornment is made a test of which people are best in deeds; it joins crafted appearance and the quality of action, while the ayah's own context emphasizes the test.
God says He does not waste the reward of anyone who does good work (“أَحْسَنَ عَمَلًا”); this is another direct formulation of the section's sound work receiving a lasting wage.
For believers who do righteous deeds, God removes their evils and “أَصْلَحَ بَالَهُمْ”; this directly develops the section's note that ص ل ح includes God's setting the human right.
After repentance, faith and righteous work, God replaces evil deeds with good ones; this is a specific repair of spoiled work, rather than a generic reference to good deeds.
Speaking rightly is followed by God's setting deeds right and forgiving sins; it directly connects sound speech, إصلاح of work and divine repair.
God's word is complete in truth and justice and no one can change it; this concretely matches the section's ح ك م definition of securing something against فساد.
The ayah says none can change God's words; it repeats the section's firm, protected work theme in the context of revelation.
There is no change in God's words; this repeated formulation supports the section's claim that the muhkam is secure from alteration.
Falsehood cannot approach the revelation from before or behind, which is from the Wise and Praiseworthy; the ayah gives a specific boundary against فساد for the section's notion of firm work.
Noah addresses God as “أَحْكَمُ الْحَاكِمِينَ”; this repeats the exact judge-formulation named in the section's 95:8 discussion, now in Noah's plea about his son.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it; this makes the section's work-and-wage claim concrete at the smallest measure.
The matching statement about an atom's weight of evil completes the exact accounting contrast between sound and spoiled work.
After the denial of recompense, the passage names guardians over people; this continues the parallel to the section by moving from fashioned humans to accountability for their deeds.
The guardians are described as noble recorders; this specifies how deeds in the neighboring judgment passage are preserved.
The recorders know what people do; this connects the section's عَمِلُوا صالحات to the accountability that follows the created-form passage.
The passage says the righteous will be in bliss; it completes the preceding record of deeds with the good outcome that parallels 95:6.
The passage says the wicked will be in Hell; this supplies the contrary outcome to the righteous and lasting reward in the section.
The wicked enter the Fire on the Day of Recompense; this continues the judgment consequence that the section raises after the crafted human's descent.
They are not absent from the Fire; this ayah specifies the permanence of the adverse outcome in the continuing passage.
The passage asks what will make one know the Day of Recompense; it completes the warning after the created and composed human, matching the section's question about denial of judgment.
The repeated question about the Day of Recompense intensifies the same warning, echoing the section's repeated challenge before God's final judgment.
On that day no soul can avail another and command belongs to God; it closes the judgment passage with the sovereign decision that matches the section's final appeal to the best of judges.

The ayah asks whether people thought they were created in vain and would not return to God; it gives a direct purpose-and-return counterpart to the section's crafted human and question about judgment.
God created heavens and earth in truth so that each soul is recompensed for what it earned; the ayah directly joins deliberate creation to measured recompense for work.
The heavens and earth were not created in play; this states that creation is purposeful, a boundary against treating the section's crafted human as an accidental or useless product.
The next ayah says they were created in truth, though most do not know; it completes 44:38 by naming the purposeful order behind creation.
The heavens and earth were not created in vain; the ayah calls that assumption the disbelievers' and links purposive making to the section's challenge about judgment.
